one_liner: Experimental AVX2/AVX-512F quicksorts for 32-bit keys; only Lemire's in-repo AVX2 variant beats std::sort on random data.
what_it_does: A research repository of vectorized in-place quicksorts for 32-bit integer arrays: Mula's AVX2 Hoare-style partition (qs::avx2::quicksort), Daniel Lemire's pivot-on-last AVX2 'alt' quicksort (avx2-altquicksort.h), two sketches of Nathan Kurz's scheme ('nate' and 'nodutch'), and AVX-512F variants (plain, popcnt, BMI2, aux-buffer) that finish partitions of 16 or fewer keys in one register. Every routine has the shape f(uint32_t* array, int left, int right) with inclusive bounds; there is no packaged header or comparator, so you copy the file you want. The Lemire and Nate variants cast the pointer to int32_t and sort in signed order (the nodutch wrapper's own comment: 'it is really signed int sorting').
how_it_is_fast: Lemire's alt quicksort compares 8 keys with the pivot in one vpcmpgtd, turns the result into an 8-bit mask with movmskps, and loads a permutation from a 256-entry table so vpermd packs the 'not greater' lanes to the front; it then stores whole vectors and advances by the popcount, a branchless Lomuto-style vector partition. Mula's qs::avx2 partition loads one vector from each end, pairs misplaced lanes with ctz loops (align_masks) and swaps them in registers, with a scalar Hoare partition for the remainder. The AVX-512F versions use mask compares and a rank-based in-register sort (avx512_sortN_epi32: permutexvar broadcast, cmplt/cmpeq popcounts, masked move) for small partitions.
when_to_use: Studying or prototyping SIMD partition schemes: each variant is a few hundred lines of nearly plain C with intrinsics.

Vendoring a small AVX2-only in-place sort for signed int32 arrays of roughly 10k to 20M elements, using avx2-altquicksort.h: 1.35x to 1.85x faster than std::sort on random keys in the issue #8 Tiger Lake run.
As an extra contender when benchmarking your own 32-bit sort against std::sort, x86-simd-sort or Highway vqsort.
Machines with AVX2 but no AVX-512 where adding a larger dependency is not an option and inputs are random rather than adversarial.
when_not_to_use: Production sorting: no introsort depth limit; qs::avx2::quicksort goes quadratic on few distinct keys (issue #1: about 9 s against under 1 s for other variants; issue #3: over 10 minutes against 6.654 s for std::sort on rand()%10 at n = 1e7), and HEAD's qs::avx512::quicksort and bmi2_quicksort take the first element as pivot, so sorted input recurses n deep (issue #4: hang, maintainer: stack runs out).

uint32_t keys at or above 2^31: every SIMD compare is signed (vpcmpgtd, _mm512_cmp*_epi32_mask); the Lemire and Nate variants return signed order, and qs::avx2 and qs::avx512 mix signed vector compares with unsigned scalar compares, so mixed-top-bit inputs come out unsorted (code reading; the tests never generate such keys because random() returns values below 2^31).
Anything other than 32-bit integer keys on x86-64 with GCC or Clang: no 64-bit keys, floats, key-value pairs or comparators, no MSVC (GCC attributes and inline asm), no ARM, no runtime CPU dispatch.

avx2-nate-quicksort.cpp ('Nate's variant'): out-of-bounds read crash at line 340 on 1M ascending keys (issue #4) and a non-terminating partition loop (issue #10, 2025); the BMI2 AVX-512 variant fails at 50M to 100M items (issue #2).
When a maintained, faster SIMD sort is acceptable: x86-simd-sort and Highway vqsort (already catalogued) supersede this 2016-2017 code.

integration.dependencies: none beyond <x86intrin.h>; the headers expect FORCE_INLINE from common.h and scalar_partition_epi32 from partition.cpp, so copy those too
integration.min_toolchain: GCC 5.3.0 or newer per the README; Makefile uses -std=c++11 -mbmi2 plus -mavx2 or -mavx512f and -O3 -DNDEBUG for the speed binary; Clang should work (GCC-style builtins), MSVC is not supported
integration.platforms: x86-64 only: AVX2 (the Makefile also passes -mbmi2) for the AVX2 variants, AVX-512F for the AVX-512 variants (the README suggests Intel SDE to run them without hardware)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; most routines touch only the caller's buffer and read-only lookup tables, but Nate's variant partitions through a function-static tmp buffer (not reentrant) and WITH_RUNTIME_STATS builds update global counters
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — sorts a raw uint32_t buffer given inclusive int bounds instead of iterators, has no comparator, caps sizes at INT_MAX elements, and the fast Lemire variant gives signed int32 order

gotchas: Benchmark harness bug: speed.cpp's PerformanceTest::run memcpy's the input into tmp but sorts input.pointer() in place, so after std::sort's first iteration every timed run (and every later algorithm) sorts presorted data; the results/ 'random' rows are presorted-data times (issues #7 and #8, open). The same file gates the scalar 'quick sort' row on the -std-qsort flag instead of -quicksort, and the measured RDTSC overhead is printed but never subtracted.

Signedness defect (code reading, not run): vector compares are signed _epi32 while partition.cpp's scalar fallback and the size-2 case compare as uint32_t, so qs::avx2::quicksort and the qs::avx512 sorts misorder arrays that mix keys below and above 2^31; the Lemire and Nate wrappers cast to int32_t and return signed order. The test program only uses random(), small ascending/descending values and random() % 10, so it cannot catch this.

Out-of-bounds access (code reading): for partitions of 16 or fewer keys, qs::avx512::quicksort and popcnt_quicksort do an unmasked 64-byte _mm512_loadu_si512 and _mm512_storeu_si512 at array + i, so the last partition reads and rewrites up to 60 bytes past the end of the caller's buffer (same bytes written back, but undefined behaviour that can fault at a page boundary); pad buffers by 64 bytes if you use them.

Worst cases are unguarded: middle-element or first-element pivots, no median-of-three, no depth limit and recursion on both sides, so adversarial, few-distinct or (for the AVX-512 variants) sorted inputs can be quadratic and exhaust the stack.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely: Bramas's avx-512-sort (AVX-512 quicksort with bitonic small-array sorts, about 4x over GNU sort in its paper) and jonicho/simd-radix-sort (about 4.1x over std::sort on uniform int32 in its thesis) are better evidenced and more complete. Pick avx2-altquicksort.h only when you need a tiny AVX2-only (no AVX-512) in-place sort for signed int32 data and cannot take x86-simd-sort or vqsort.
verified_claims_summary: The repo's own results/ files (GCC 5.3.0 on i7-6700, i7-4770 and Xeon Phi 7210, 2016) are invalid because the harness re-sorted presorted data. With the harness fixed, a third party (issue #8, Tiger Lake, CentOS 8, compiler unstated, RDTSC minimum of N runs, random() keys) measured Lemire's AVX2 alt quicksort at 1.61x, 1.77x, 1.82x and 1.85x the speed of libstdc++ std::sort at 1M, 2M, 10M and 20M keys, the nodutch variant at 1.23x to 1.38x, and Mula's qs::avx2::quicksort at 0.84x to 0.92x (slower); an independent run in issue #3 (simonlindholm, i5-4200U, g++ 5.4 -std=c++11 -O3 -march=native, sum of 20 sorts of 1e7 keys) found qs::avx2::quicksort at 19.476 s against std::sort's 20.209 s on random input (about 1.04x, derived from page data) and over 10 minutes against 6.654 s on rand()%10.
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-11-22 (the last commit only fixed a t1/t2 typo in the gettimeofday branch), BSD-2-Clause and small enough to vendor, but research code with an invalid benchmark harness, signed-compare and out-of-bounds defects found in code reading, and quadratic worst cases; the issue #3 run, which the verifier did not cite, confirms the headline AVX2 quicksort is only at parity with std::sort on random data and collapses on few distinct keys.
